mainTopic: A recipient who refuses a gift (the dispute of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן), and how a שכיב מרע's wording sets the priority and meaning of his gifts
overview: This amud opens by finishing an answer to a contradiction between a ruling of רבי יוחנן and one of שמואל about a person who refuses a gift. If he protests right away, he never acquires it. If he is silent at first and protests only later, it is already his. רב נחמן בר יצחק adds that a gift acquired for him through a middleman, where he was silent and later protested, is the case argued in a ברייתא about gifted slaves. In that ברייתא, the תנא קמא says the slaves still belong to the recipient, so they may eat תרומה if he is a כהן. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the refusal works and the heirs keep them. The גמרא explains that the תנא קמא sees the later protest as backing out. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the protest shows the recipient never agreed. Next come ברייתות about a שכיב מרע's gifts. A plain list of gifts gives no one priority, but 'and after him' does, so a creditor collects from the last-named recipient first. A gift to a בכור or a wife 'as is fitting' comes on top of the בכורה or כתובה. A gift 'for his בכורה' lets the son choose one. The wife's parallel case continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Protesting right away versus protesting later
steps.stepSummary: The two rulings speak about different cases. In one, the recipient protests from the start. In the other, he was silent at first and protested only later.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, it is where he shouts in protest from the very start. There, it is where he was silent at first and only shouted later.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to a contradiction between two rulings about a recipient who refuses a gift. It says each ruling deals with a different timing of the protest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the recipient objects the moment the gift reaches him, it never becomes his. If he stays quiet when he receives it, he acquires it right then. A later protest cannot undo a gift that is already his. So the two rulings do not argue; they describe two different cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Shouts or protests, here saying 'I don't want this gift'
From the start, right away
Is silent, says nothing
In the end, later on

steps.whatToRemember: Silence when the gift arrives means the recipient acquired it. Only a protest right at the start stops the gift.
steps.confusionAlert: This line does not start a new topic. It is the end of an answer to a contradiction raised just before this section, so 'here' and 'there' point back to the two rulings that clashed.

phrases.english: Here, it is where he shouts in protest from the start,
phrases.notes: 'Here' is רבי יוחנן's ruling (no acquisition), and 'there' is שמואל's ruling (he acquires), the two rulings that clashed just before.

phrases.english: there, it is where he is silent at the start
and in the end shouts in protest.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּאן בְּצוֹוֵחַ מֵעִיקָּרָא, כָּאן בְּשׁוֹתֵק מֵעִיקָּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves a contradiction raised just before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each ruling deals with a different timing of the protest.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two rulings seemed to contradict each other about whether a refusing recipient acquires the gift.
steps.terutzMaskana: A protest right away blocks the gift. Silence first, then protest, means the gift was already acquired.

steps.title: A gift given through a middleman links to a famous dispute
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says: if the gift was acquired for the recipient through someone else, and he was silent and later protested, this case is the מחלוקת between רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: If the giver transferred the gift to him through another person, and he was silent and later protested, we have reached the dispute of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק adds a new case: the gift was acquired for the recipient by a middleman. He says this case is not simple; it depends on an older מחלוקת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 dealt with a recipient who received the gift himself. Here someone else accepted it on his behalf, and he only protested when he found out. Whether his later protest counts depends on the dispute that the next step quotes.

keyTerms.meaning: Transferred ownership, gave someone legal possession
Through another person, a middleman who accepts for him
A dispute between authorities

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the clear rule from step 1 does not settle every case. When a middleman is involved, the answer depends on whose view we follow.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
If he transferred it to him through another person,
and he was silent and in the end protested,
we have arrived at the dispute
of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the 'silent then protests' case from step 1 and applies it to a gift acquired through a middleman.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gift acquired through a middleman, where the recipient was silent and later protested, depends on the מחלוקת of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the רבנן.

steps.title: The ברייתא about gifted slaves and תרומה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא: someone wrote his property to another, including slaves, and the recipient said 'I don't want them.' The תנא קמא says they still belong to him and eat תרומה if he is a כהן. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the heirs already acquired them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: One who writes his property to another, and there were slaves in it, and that person said 'I don't want them.' If their second master was a כהן, they eat תרומה. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Once that person said 'I don't want them,' the heirs have already acquired them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא that contains the dispute רב נחמן בר יצחק mentioned. This is the source behind his statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slaves eating תרומה is a test of who owns them, because a כהן's slaves may eat תרומה. The תנא קמא says they eat, so the recipient owns them despite his refusal. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the refusal works, so they never left the original side.

keyTerms.meaning: One who writes over his property in a document
I don't want them
The holy portion of produce given to a כהן
Heirs
As it was taught in a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never mentions a middleman. רב נחמן בר יצחק is the one who reads it as his middleman case.

phrases.english: As it is taught: One who writes his property over to another,
and there were slaves among it,
and that person said: 'I don't want them';
if their second master was a priest,
phrases.notes: 'Second master' means the person who received the slaves as a gift.

phrases.english: they eat teruma.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
Once that person said: 'I don't want them,'
the heirs have already acquired them.
phrases.notes: The giver's heirs, meaning the slaves stay on the giver's side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the ברייתא that step 2 refers to.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן בר יצחק's claim that the middleman case (silent at first, protesting later) is exactly what the תנא קמא and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל argue about. Steps 5-7 show that the ברייתא's dispute is limited to that case.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא (תוספתא בבא בתרא 8:1) about gifted slaves and eating תרומה.

steps.title: Does the תנא קמא really ignore a loud protest?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the ברייתא: could the תנא קמא hold that the recipient acquires the slaves even while he stands there protesting?
steps.simpleTranslation: And we discussed it: And does the תנא קמא hold that he acquires them even if he is standing and shouting in protest?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to challenge the plain reading of the ברייתא. This sets up the next move, an explanation of what case the תנא קמא means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It makes no sense to force a gift on someone who loudly refuses it. So the תנא קמא's view as written seems too extreme. The גמרא will need to explain it in a narrower way.

keyTerms.meaning: And we discussed it, introducing an earlier question on this source
The first, unnamed teacher in a ברייתא or משנה
Standing and shouting in protest

phrases.english: And we discussed it:
And the first tanna,
even if he is standing and shouting?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָוֵינַן בַּהּ: וְתַנָּא קַמָּא אֲפִילּוּ עוֹמֵד וְצוֹוֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תנא קמא's view in the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The תנא קמא's ruling that the slaves eat תרומה despite the refusal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read plainly, the תנא קמא would force a gift on someone actively protesting. That seems unreasonable, and step 1 already said a protest right away blocks the gift.

steps.title: Two cases where everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: רבא (or רבי יוחנן) sets out two clear cases. Protesting from the start means no acquisition, by everyone's opinion. Silence first and protest later means acquisition, by everyone's opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said, and some say it was רבי יוחנן: If he shouts in protest from the very beginning, everyone agrees he does not acquire. If he was silent and only shouted later, everyone agrees he does acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 4 by first pointing out two cases where there is no argument at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 asked how the תנא קמא could say a man owns slaves while he is standing there protesting. רבא answers that nobody holds that, since protesting from the start means no acquisition, by everyone's opinion. So the ברייתא's argument must be about a different, in-between case, which comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say: the statement is also reported in the name of someone else
Shouts in protest from the very start
Was silent, and only later shouted in protest
Everyone agrees, so there is no argument here
Acquires, becomes the owner

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. Protesting right away means he is not the owner. Being silent and protesting later means he is the owner, by everyone's opinion, unless the special case in the next step applies.

phrases.english: Rava said, and some say it was Rabbi Yochanan:
Where he shouts in protest from the very start,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּלָא קָנֵי.
phrases.english: everyone agrees that he does not acquire.
If he was silent and in the end shouted,
everyone agrees that he acquires.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בְּצוֹוֵחַ מֵעִיקָּרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the קשיא of step 4 by removing the 'protesting from the start' case from the מחלוקת.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the מחלוקת
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא seemed to hold that a recipient acquires even while protesting from the start.
steps.terutzMaskana: When he protests from the start, no one holds he acquires. When he is silent and then protests, everyone holds he acquires.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Protest from the start means no acquisition. Silence followed by protest means acquisition. Both cases are agreed by all.

steps.title: Where they argue, and the view of the תנא קמא
steps.stepSummary: The מחלוקת is where the gift was transferred through another person, the recipient was silent, and he protested later. The תנא קמא says his silence made him the owner, and his protest is just backing out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where they argue is when he gave it to him through another person, and the recipient was silent and only shouted later. The תנא קמא holds: since he was silent, he acquired them, and his shouting now is just him backing out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now identifies the exact case the ברייתא is arguing about and explains the תנא קמא's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the gift came through a middleman (זיכוי על ידי אחר), and the recipient protested only later. The תנא קמא treats his first silence as acceptance, so ownership already took hold. A later protest cannot undo an acquisition that is already complete; it is simply changing his mind.

keyTerms.meaning: He transferred ownership to him through another person, a middleman
The first, unnamed opinion in the ברייתא
He acquired them
He backed out, changed his mind

phrases.english: Where they disagree
is when he transferred it to him through another person
and he was silent, and in the end shouted;
for the first Tanna holds:
since he was silent, he acquired them;
and the fact that he is shouting
is just that he is backing out.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי – שֶׁזִּיכָּה לוֹ עַל יְדֵי אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer begun in step 5 by naming the case where the two opinions really argue, and gives the תנא קמא's reasoning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the case of the מחלוקת
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be about someone protesting right from the start.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about a gift given through a middleman, where the recipient was silent first and protested only later. The תנא קמא says the silence already made him the owner.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, silence at the time of a gift through a middleman counts as acceptance, and a later protest is only backing out.

steps.title: The view of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the later protest shows he never wanted them. He kept quiet only because the slaves were not yet in his hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds: his end shows what he meant at the beginning. The reason he did not shout until now is that he thought: as long as they have not come into my hands, why should I shout?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the other side of the מחלוקת: why רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the recipient never acquired.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל reads the later protest backwards: it shows that the earlier silence was never agreement. The silence is explained away, since there was no reason to object before the slaves actually reached him. So the slaves stay with the giver's heirs, as the ברייתא said.

keyTerms.meaning: His end shows what he meant at the beginning
Until now
They reached my hands, came into my possession

steps.whatToRemember: Silence first and protest later, with the gift given through a middleman: the תנא קמא says the silence was acceptance and the protest is backing out. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the protest shows he never agreed, and he was quiet only because nothing had reached him yet.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows two ways of reading silence: as agreement, or as simply waiting until there is something to object to.

phrases.english: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds:
his end shows what he meant at the beginning;
and the fact that he did not shout until now
is because he thought: as long as they have not reached my hands,
why should I shout?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל סָבַר: הוֹכִיחַ סוֹפוֹ עַל תְּחִלָּתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the מחלוקת defined in step 6, finishing the answer to the קשיא of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the reasoning of the other opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His early silence might seem to be clear acceptance of the gift.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the later protest shows he never accepted, and the early silence is explained away.

steps.title: Several gifts from a dying man: no one comes first
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: a שכיב מרע lists several money gifts. Being named first does not give priority, so a creditor of the giver collects from all of the recipients.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A שכיב מרע said, 'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so, three hundred to so-and-so, and four hundred to so-and-so.' We do not say that whoever is named first in the document gets it first. Therefore, if a debt document against the giver comes out, the creditor collects from all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא about the gifts of a שכיב מרע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שכיב מרע's gifts all take effect together, at his death, so the order in which he lists them does not matter. Because of that, no recipient gets priority over the others. If a creditor later shows up, he cannot be pushed onto only the last-named recipient; he collects from all of them.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught: introduces a ברייתא
A person who is dangerously ill, on his deathbed, whose spoken gifts take effect
So-and-so
The one who comes first in the document
A document recording a loan
Collects payment

steps.confusionAlert: Normally a creditor collects from whatever was sold or given away last. Here there is no 'last', because all the gifts count as given at the same moment.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A dying man who said:
"Give two hundred zuz to so-and-so,
and three hundred to so-and-so,
and four hundred to so-and-so"

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אוֹמְרִין: כׇּל הַקּוֹדֵם בִּשְׁטָר, זוֹכֶה.
phrases.english: we do not say: whoever comes first in the document acquires first.
Therefore, if a debt document came out against him,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the dying man who gave the gifts.

phrases.english: the creditor collects from all of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the protesting recipient has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The listed gifts of a שכיב מרע have no order of priority, so a creditor collects from all of the recipients.

steps.title: Saying 'and after him' gives priority to whoever is named first
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא now gives the opposite case to step 8. When the שכיב מרע chains the gifts with 'and after him,' whoever appears first in the document has priority.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said: 'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so, and after him to so-and-so, and after him to so-and-so,' we say that whoever comes first in the document gains.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues from step 8. It shows a different way of wording the gifts that does create an order of priority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8 the names were just listed, so nobody came 'first,' and a creditor collected from all of them equally. Here the words 'and after him' (וְאַחֲרָיו) set up a ranking. So the person named earlier has the stronger claim.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And after him': wording that puts the recipients in an order
Whoever comes first in the document gains
A silver coin; 200 זוז is the sum in these cases

phrases.english: But if he said:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the שכיב מרע from step 8.

phrases.english: 'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so,
and after him to so-and-so, and after him to so-and-so' –
we say: whoever comes first in the document gains.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case to the plain list in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When gifts are chained with 'and after him,' the person named first has priority.

steps.title: A creditor collects from the last recipient first
steps.stepSummary: Because the earlier recipient has priority, a creditor of the giver collects from the last-named recipient first, then moves backward up the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore, if a debt document comes out against the giver, the creditor collects from the last one. If that one does not have enough, he collects from the one before him. If he does not have enough, he collects from the one before that.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the practical result of the order set up in step 9. It tells us how a creditor collects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having priority means you are the last one to lose your gift. So the creditor starts with the lowest-ranked recipient, the last one named, and moves up the list only if he still has not been paid. This is the opposite of step 8, where everyone shared the loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore: this is the result of the rule just stated
A document that proves a debt
Collects payment
From the one before the previous one

steps.whatToRemember: A plain list means everyone is equal (step 8). 'And after him' sets an order, so the creditor collects from the last-named recipient first.

phrases.english: Therefore, if a debt document came out against him,
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the giver, the man who died owing money.

phrases.english: he collects from the last one.
If he does not have enough, he collects from the one before him.
If he does not have enough, he collects from the one before that.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the practical result of the priority set up in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The creditor collects in reverse order, starting from the last-named recipient.

steps.title: A gift to the firstborn: 'as is fitting for him' versus 'for his בכורה'
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא. If a שכיב מרע gives 200 זוז to his בכור 'as is fitting for him,' the son gets both the money and his בכורה. If he says 'for his בכורה,' the son chooses one or the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: a שכיב מרע said, 'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so, my firstborn son, as is fitting for him.' The son takes the money and also takes his בכורה. If he said 'for his בכורה,' the son has the upper hand: if he wants, he takes the money, and if he wants, he takes his בכורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the gifts of a שכיב מרע. Here the gift goes to his firstborn son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'As is fitting for him' (כָּרָאוּי לוֹ) is read as just a friendly reason for the gift. So the money is an extra gift on top of his בכורה. 'For his בכורה' (בִּבְכוֹרָתוֹ) means the money is meant to replace his בכורה. Still, he is not forced to accept the swap, so he picks whichever is worth more to him.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן taught: this opens a ברייתא
Firstborn son, who gets a double share of the inheritance
As is fitting for him
His firstborn's portion (בכורה)
He has the upper hand: he gets to choose

steps.confusionAlert: In the second case the son does NOT get both. He picks one, either the 200 זוז or his בכורה.

phrases.english: The רבנן taught:
A sick man on his deathbed who said:
'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so, my firstborn son,
as is fitting for him' –
he takes them, and he takes his firstborn's portion too.
If he said: 'for his firstborn's portion' –
he has the upper hand;
if he wants, he takes the money; if he wants, he takes his firstborn's portion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא on the gifts of a שכיב מרע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'As is fitting for him' means he gets both. 'For his בכורה' means he chooses one.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the exact wording of a gift decides whether it is extra or a replacement for something the person already has coming to him.

steps.title: The same rule for a wife and her כתובה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא applies the same pattern to a wife. If he says 'as is fitting for her,' she takes the 200 זוז and her כתובה. Then it starts the case where he said 'for her כתובה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And a שכיב מרע who said, 'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so, my wife, as is fitting for her': she takes the money and also takes her כתובה. If he said 'for her כתובה' –
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא repeats the firstborn pattern, this time for a wife. Her ruling for 'for her כתובה' continues past the end of this text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too, 'as is fitting for her' makes the money an extra gift on top of her כתובה. The case of 'for her כתובה' parallels the בכורה case, but the ruling itself is not in this text.

keyTerms.meaning: My wife
Her כתובה: the money a wife collects under her marriage contract
She takes them

phrases.english: And a sick man on his deathbed who said:
'Give two hundred זוז to so-and-so, my wife,
as is fitting for her' –
she takes them, and she takes her כתובה too.
If he said 'for her כתובה' –

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁכִיב מְרַע שֶׁאָמַר: תְּנוּ מָאתַיִם זוּז לִפְלוֹנִית אִשְׁתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the firstborn wording rule from step 11 to a wife's כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'As is fitting for her' means she gets the 200 זוז as well as her כתובה.
